title: Jeremiah 43:1–13
context: Azariah, Johanan, and the proud men reject Jeremiah’s message as a lie and blame Baruch. Johanan and the captains take the whole remnant, including Jeremiah and Baruch, to Egypt, as far as Tahpanhes; 2 Kings 25:26 also records the flight to Egypt. There the LORD tells Jeremiah to hide large stones at the entrance of Pharaoh’s house as a sign that Nebuchadnezzar will come, set his throne over them, and strike Egypt and its gods. Site identifications and archaeological links should be held cautiously. Both traditions read the passage as shared ground about disobedience and the futility of seeking refuge apart from God.

verses.text: When Jeremiah had finished speaking to all the people all the words of the LORD their God, with which the LORD their God had sent him to them, even all these words,
verses.arminianNotes:
When Jeremiah finishes speaking all the LORD’s words to the people, the response follows. The narrator marks the moment.

Arminian readers see a people who have now heard everything and must decide how they will answer God’s word.
verses.reformedNotes:
The narrator stresses that Jeremiah delivered “all these words,” leaving nothing out.

Reformed readers see God’s full counsel faithfully declared. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the prophet’s faithfulness and the people’s full knowledge of what God required.

verses.text: then Azariah the son of Hoshaiah, Johanan the son of Kareah, and all the proud men spoke, saying to Jeremiah, “You speak falsely. The LORD our God has not sent you to say, ‘You shall not go into Egypt to live there;’
verses.arminianNotes:
Azariah son of Hoshaiah, Johanan, and all the proud men tell Jeremiah, “You speak falsely,” denying that the LORD sent him. Pride rejects the word.

Arminian readers see a deliberate refusal.
verses.reformedNotes:
Chapter 42:1 names Jezaniah son of Hoshaiah, while 43:2 names Azariah son of Hoshaiah; the text does not explain the difference.

Reformed readers see proud hearts resisting God. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: but Baruch the son of Neriah has turned you against us, to deliver us into the hand of the Chaldeans, that they may put us to death or carry us away captive to Babylon.”
verses.arminianNotes:
They claim Baruch son of Neriah has turned Jeremiah against them, to hand them to the Chaldeans for death or exile. Blame shifts to Baruch.

Arminian readers see suspicion used to avoid an unwelcome command.
verses.reformedNotes:
The accusation implies that Baruch had influence over Jeremiah, a claim the text presents as unfounded.

Reformed readers see the ways people evade God’s word by attacking its messengers. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the danger of dismissing truth by questioning motives.

verses.text: So Johanan the son of Kareah, and all the captains of the forces, and all the people, didn’t obey the LORD’s voice, to dwell in the land of Judah.
verses.arminianNotes:
Johanan, the captains, and all the people do not obey the LORD’s voice to stay in Judah. The decision is made.

Arminian readers see a collective, chosen disobedience after a clear warning, despite the oath they had sworn in 42:5–6.
verses.reformedNotes:
The narrator states the outcome plainly, echoing 42:21.

Reformed readers see the persistence of unbelief. Both traditions read this as shared ground about disobedience to God’s clear word and the community’s responsibility for its choice.

verses.text: But Johanan the son of Kareah and all the captains of the forces took all the remnant of Judah, who had returned from all the nations where they had been driven, to live in the land of Judah—
verses.arminianNotes:
Johanan and the captains take the whole remnant of Judah, including those who had returned from the nations where they were scattered. The community is uprooted.

Arminian readers see leaders drawing others into their decision.
verses.reformedNotes:
Some had returned to Judah after scattering (compare 40:11–12), only to be taken away again.

Reformed readers see the tragedy of a remnant leaving the land. Both traditions read this as shared ground about leaders’ responsibility for those they lead.

verses.text: the men, the women, the children, the king’s daughters, and every person who Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard had left with Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, the son of Shaphan; and Jeremiah the prophet, and Baruch the son of Neriah.
verses.arminianNotes:
Men, women, children, the king’s daughters, and all whom Nebuzaradan left with Gedaliah are taken, along with Jeremiah and Baruch. Even the prophet goes.

Arminian readers see Jeremiah sharing the consequences of others’ choices.
verses.reformedNotes:
The text does not say whether Jeremiah and Baruch went willingly; it lists them among those taken.

Reformed readers see God’s servant remaining with his people. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: They came into the land of Egypt, for they didn’t obey the LORD’s voice; and they came to Tahpanhes.
verses.arminianNotes:
They enter Egypt, disobeying the LORD’s voice, and come to Tahpanhes. The journey ends in disobedience.

Arminian readers see the narrator underlining the people’s choice once again, as the remnant settles in the very place God had warned them against.
verses.reformedNotes:
Tahpanhes is usually placed in the eastern Nile Delta, though its exact identification is debated. 2 Kings 25:26 also reports the flight to Egypt for fear of the Chaldeans.

Reformed readers see unbelief carried to its end. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: Then the LORD’s word came to Jeremiah in Tahpanhes, saying,
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD’s word comes to Jeremiah in Tahpanhes. God still speaks in Egypt.

Arminian readers see God continuing to address his people even after they have disobeyed and left the land.
verses.reformedNotes:
The location shows that God’s word is not confined to Judah.

Reformed readers see God’s sovereignty extending to Egypt. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the reach of God’s word, which follows the people even into the place they chose against his command.

verses.text: “Take great stones in your hand and hide them in mortar in the brick work which is at the entry of Pharaoh’s house in Tahpanhes, in the sight of the men of Judah.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD tells Jeremiah to take large stones and hide them in mortar in the brickwork at the entrance of Pharaoh’s house in Tahpanhes, in the sight of the men of Judah. A sign is enacted.

Arminian readers see a visible warning to the people.
verses.reformedNotes:
The building described as Pharaoh’s house may have been a royal or official residence; claims linking it to specific excavated remains should be held cautiously.

Reformed readers see God’s word made visible. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: Tell them, the LORD of Armies, the God of Israel, says: ‘Behold, I will send and take Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon, my servant, and will set his throne on these stones that I have hidden; and he will spread his royal pavilion over them.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jeremiah is to say that the LORD will bring Nebuchadnezzar, “my servant,” and set his throne over these stones and spread his royal pavilion over them. Babylon will reach Egypt.

Arminian readers see God using a foreign ruler for his purposes.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calling Nebuchadnezzar “my servant” recalls 25:9; on God working through foreign rulers and agents, compare Judges 9:23.

Reformed readers see God directing nations. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: He will come, and will strike the land of Egypt; such as are for death will be put to death, and such as are for captivity to captivity, and such as are for the sword to the sword.
verses.arminianNotes:
Nebuchadnezzar will strike Egypt; some to death, some to captivity, some to the sword. Judgment comes to Egypt.

Arminian readers see the security the people sought in Egypt proven false.
verses.reformedNotes:
The pattern of death, captivity, and sword echoes 15:2. Chapter 46:13–26 also announces Nebuchadnezzar’s coming against Egypt.

Reformed readers see God’s word extending to the nations. Both traditions read this as shared ground and hold historical reconstructions of the campaign tentatively.

verses.text: I will kindle a fire in the houses of the gods of Egypt. He will burn them, and carry them away captive. He will array himself with the land of Egypt, as a shepherd puts on his garment; and he will go out from there in peace.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD will kindle fire in the temples of Egypt’s gods; Nebuchadnezzar will burn them, carry them off, and wrap himself in Egypt like a shepherd in his cloak. The gods cannot protect.

Arminian readers see the futility of trust in other gods.
verses.reformedNotes:
The shepherd image pictures ease of conquest.

Reformed readers see God’s supremacy over the gods of the nations. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the powerlessness of idols, which anticipates the dispute of chapter 44.

verses.text: He will also break the pillars of Beth Shemesh that is in the land of Egypt; and he will burn the houses of the gods of Egypt with fire.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes:
He will break the pillars of Beth Shemesh in Egypt and burn the houses of Egypt’s gods. The oracle closes.

Arminian readers see the end of Egypt’s religious confidence before the LORD’s purpose.
verses.reformedNotes:
Beth Shemesh in Egypt is often identified with the city known as Heliopolis, though this identification should be held with caution.

Reformed readers see God’s judgment on idolatry. Both traditions read this as shared ground and keep the site identification hedged.
